title: DCPSC Order No. 22890 (2026-06-30) — The Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia, in Formal Case Nos. 977, 1178, and GD-2026-02-M, by Order No. 22890, dated June 30, 2026, among other
description: The Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia, in Formal Case Nos. 977, 1178, and GD-2026-02-M, by Order No. 22890, dated June 30, 2026, among other things, granted the Office of the People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia’s (“OPC”) motion for status and held in abeyance the OPC petition to establish an independent distribution monitor to evaluate and oversee Washington Gas’s recordings, reporting, and maintenance of gas leak data.

1325 G STREET, N.W., SUITE 800 
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20005 
ORDER

FORMAL CASE NO. 977, IN THE MATTER OF THE INVESTIGATION INTO THE 
QUALITY OF SERVICE OF WASHINGTON GAS LIGHT COMPANY, 
FORMAL CASE NO. 1178, IN THE MATTER OF PETITION FOR INVESTIGATION 
INTO WASHINGTON GAS LIGHT COMPANY’S SYSTEM LEAK REDUCTION 
PRACTICES,

GD-2026-02-M, IN THE MATTER OF THE PETITION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF 
AN INDEPENDENT DISTRIBUTION MONITOR TO EVALUATE AND OVERSEE 
WGL’S RECORDINGS, REPORTING, AND MAINTENANCE OF GAS LEAK DATA, 
Order No. 22890 
I.
INTRODUCTION
1.
By this Order, the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia
(“Commission”) grants the Office of People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia’s (“OPC”) 
motion for status and holds in abeyance the OPC petition to establish an Independent Distribution 
Monitor (“IDM”) to evaluate and oversee Washington Gas Light Company’s (“WGL” or 
“Company”) recordings, reporting, and maintenance of gas leak data in the District of Columbia 
(“District”). WGL is directed to hold the last series of technical conferences on leak mapping and 
Geospatial Information Systems (“GIS”) in Formal Case No. 1178 within 45 days of the date of 
this order, and technical conferences in Formal Case No. 977 shall continue as scheduled by the 
Commission. This Order also directs WGL and stakeholders to file a joint report in Formal Case 
No. 1178 within 180 days of the date of this Order. 
II.
BACKGROUND
2.
Through Order No. 22004, the Commission granted, in part, and denied, in part,
OPC's request to investigate WGL’s distribution system leak reduction system. 1 The investigation 
was directed to cover leak reduction practices, leak detection methods, WGL’s protocols on leak 
identification, reporting, and mapping for leaks and repairs.2 The investigation is nearing its end, 
with a final technical conference planned during which WGL is expected to present on leak

mapping. After the final technical conference is completed, the Commission will review the 
findings stated in the Formal Case No. 1178 Report. 

3. 
While the investigation in Formal Case No. 1178 progressed, the Commission also 
initiated a review of WGL’s repeated violations of the Natural Gas Quality of Service Standards 
(“NGQSS”) and recurring inconsistencies in data reporting.3 The Commission intended to conduct 
three technical conferences to resolve the issues noted in Order No. 2246; however, additional 
technical conferences have been necessary to properly address issues with WGL’s data reporting 
practices, which have been the subject of repeated penalties.4 

4. 
On March 19, 2026, OPC filed a petition to establish an IDM to evaluate and 
oversee the recording, reporting, and maintenance of WGL’s gas leak data in the District.5 On 
April 17, 2026, WGL filed a response to OPC’s petition.6 On June 25, 2026, OPC filed a motion 
for status on its March 19 petition and requested that the Commission issue a decision and next 
steps concerning OPC’s March 19 petition to establish an IDM.7 

III. 
DISCUSSION 

5. 
OPC’s Petition. OPC’s petition to establish an IDM argues that WGL cannot 
guarantee that it is furnishing gas in a manner that promotes the public interest, preserves public 
health, and prioritizes safety because WGL’s gas leak data lacks integrity.8 Therefore, OPC 
requests that the Commission establish an IDM to provide a level of oversight that will restore 
public confidence, ensure accountability, and maintain accurate information for regulators and 
policymakers to evaluate. 9

and Maintenance of Gas Leak Data in the District of Columbia, filed March 19, 2026 (“OPC’s Petition for an IDM”).

6. 
OPC states that it conducted an investigation into WGL’s compliance with the 
Commission’s Chapter 37 regulations on NGQSS and found 1,623 violations of 15 DCMR § 3702 
across calendar years 2023 to 2025.10 OPC notes systemic structural deficiencies that affect every 
graded gas leak in WGL’s Leak Identification, Detection and Repair, and Odor Complaints 
(“LIDAROC”) filings that have a cascading effect on the errors found throughout WGL’s data.11 
OPC found 78 LIDAROC data entries that disappeared in subsequent filings and 21 LIDAROC 
data entries that exist in weekly downgrade repair reports but are absent from WGL’s calendar year 
2025 Quarter 4 LIDAROC report.12 OPC also found 17 gas leak records in LIDAROC missing 
the required DCMR data field, eight leaks incorrectly marked as “WORK IN PROGRESS,” and 
nine graded leaks lacking a valid “LEAK_CAUSE” which all prevented OPC from conducting 
proper review and identification of repair progress.13 OPC also identified broader systemic 
deficiencies: every graded leak from calendar years 2023-2025 is missing the required response 
time and code number fields, affecting 6,224 graded leaks in that period.14 OPC states that 83.2% 
of graded leaks from calendar years 2023 and 2024 contain mathematically inconsistent repair 
times.15 While these inconsistencies were generally corrected in calendar year 2025, earlier data 
remains uncorrected, preventing the interpretation of longitudinal trend information.16 

7. 
The largest category of errors by volume that OPC identified was contradictions or 
conflicts between LIDAROC data and data from other mandated filings.17 OPC states that WGL 
recorded “NO LEAK FOUND” as the action taken for 1,241 leaks that had already been graded, 
creating an internal contradiction that renders the “ACTION_TAKEN” field unreliable, affecting 
numerous Grade 1 leaks each year, creating serious concerns about whether the most hazardous 
leaks were actually resolved.18 OPC asserts that it found 266 instances of conflicting information 
between quarterly LIDAROC reports and weekly reports required by 15 DCMR § 3702.6, with 
139 conflicts occurring in 2024 and 127 in 2025, demonstrating WGL’s failure to comply with at 
least one reporting obligation.19 OPC argues that WGL’s consistent reporting discrepancies, 
combined with persistently high annual violation totals, demonstrate systemic data integrity

8. 
OPC continues by discussing the scope and role of the IDM. OPC states that 
establishing an IDM is within the Commission’s authority and similar to actions the Commission 
has routinely taken with respect to management audits for the Potomac Electric Power Company 
(“Pepco”).22 OPC states that the IDM would evaluate the extent of missing data, analyze the 
integrity of WGL’s gas leak reporting, evaluate WGL’s data entry processes, assess the plausibility 
of stream-lining data collection and processing, identify WGL’s metrics for reliability, assess the 
plausibility of a live data dashboard, propose remedial measures for inconsistent data reported, 
determine WGL’s capability to identify a gas leak’s data cycle, review WGL’s management 
decisions and actions concerning gas leak data, and file monthly reports on the IDM’s expert 
evaluation.23 OPC states that the IDM would stand in the shoes of the Commission and be entitled 
to see any document, information, or materials that the Commission would be entitled to review 
in order to provide the information and expert judgment needed to promptly and efficiently 
evaluate WGL’s actions and decisions.24 OPC also requests that the IDM costs should be excluded 
from any rate cases because these costs are required to remediate the utility’s failure to fulfill its 
obligations in a reasonable and prudent manner.25 

9. 
OPC asserts that WGL continues to file inaccurate LIDAROC reports after the 
Commission opened an investigation; therefore, OPC believes the Commission and OPC need to 
rely on a third-party IDM to fix the inaccuracies of WGL’s leak data reporting.26 OPC further 
argues that the IDM is necessary because directing WGL to comply with LIDAROC reporting 
requirements under the risk of penalties has not worked, and yet, the underlying data remains 
important to understand the health and safety risks associated with leaks on WGL’s distribution 
system.27 OPC states that due to WGL’s failure to comply with 15 DCMR §§ 3701 and 3702, 
neither the Commission nor OPC has ever received a full accounting of gas leaks that existed in 
the District in any calendar year or the actions WGL took to address them.28 OPC further states

10. 
WGL’s Response. WGL’s response to OPC’s petition states that it does not oppose 
the appointment of an IDM; however, WGL requests that the Commission address several issues

to take action to maintain and improve the safety and reliability of its natural gas distribution in 
the District.34 WGL also acknowledges the precedent of the Commission's appointment of 
independent monitors through management audits conducted in Formal Case Nos. 1115 and 
1154.35

IV. 
DECISION 

16. 
The Commission’s authority to establish the IDM is well established and not a point 
of disagreement between OPC and WGL. Both parties cite prior examples of the Commission 
appointing an agent to review the practices of both Pepco and WGL. Both parties also 
acknowledge that the Commission has the authority to employ an agent to assist in the performance 
of the Commission’s duties to ensure that public utilities are furnishing service and facilities in a 
reasonably safe and adequate manner. The Commission’s oversight also includes evaluating the 
operational necessity and cost-effectiveness of such an appointment to protect ratepayer interests. 
However, before the Commission evaluates the merits of an IDM, WGL, and stakeholders must 
fulfill procedural prerequisites by concluding technical conferences within Formal Case Nos. 977 
and 1178 and submit joint, formal recommendations for natural gas distribution system monitoring 
as described herein. Accordingly, the Commission directs WGL and stakeholders to complete the 
technical conferences in Formal Case Nos. 977 and 1178, and present recommendations on the 
next steps for natural gas distribution system monitoring within 180 days of the date of this Order. 
Upon receipt and review of the stakeholders' joint recommendations, the Commission will assess 
whether an IDM framework represents a necessary and cost-effective mechanism for ratepayers. 

17. 
The primary concern that the Commission finds with OPC’s petition is that it would 
result in duplicative reviews of information already before the Commission. The Commission has 
two ongoing proceedings that cover the topics of the petition. In Formal Case No. 977, the 
Commission established the LIDAROC and NGQSS rules, which OPC alleges WGL has violated. 
The Commission has noted substantial issues with LIDAROC compliance and has initiated 
technical conferences to address them, and has fined the Company for its non-compliance.61 The 
Commission held a technical conference in Formal Case No. 977 as recently as June 15, 2026, 
during which OPC, WGL, and Commission Staff continued the discussion of issues with 
LIDAROC reporting. The Commission expects to use the discussions held in the Formal Case 
No. 977 technical conferences to inform any necessary revisions to the NGQSS and LIDAROC 
rules. Operating concurrently in a separate proceeding, Formal Case No. 1178, the Commission 
has required WGL to present information at technical conferences to facilitate OPC’s prior request 
to investigate WGL’s leak reduction practices. The most recent technical conference in Formal 
Case No. 1178 was held on March 12, 2026, during which stakeholders discussed capabilities for 
mapping leaks in GIS in another jurisdiction. At that technical conference, WGL committed to 
providing a timeline for scheduling the next one, but no technical conference has been held since 
then.62 The Commission notes that the investigation in Formal Case No. 1178 cannot be considered 
complete until WGL has presented on leak mapping and GIS and submitted a joint final report 
alongside stakeholders as required by Order No. 22004. 

18. 
At the technical conferences in Formal Case No. 1178, the stakeholders raised 
pertinent concerns about WGL’s leak detection practices, which relate to focal areas in this

proceeding. The Commission wants to review these concerns holistically before making a final 
determination on the IDM and WGL’s leak survey, reporting, and management practices. 

19. 
The Commission appreciates OPC's efforts to catalog and investigate WGL’s 
NGQSS and LIDAROC reports. However, we are not convinced that OPC’s report accurately 
reflects the issues with WGL’s recordkeeping practices. The Commission notes that the 
investigative report attached to OPC’s petition is based on information from Formal Case Nos. 
977 and 1178, and mandated reporting requirements. The investigative report captures issues that 
the Commission is currently addressing through the aforementioned proceedings. The Commission 
notes that OPC’s investigation report identified concerns related to leak reporting consistency, 
complaint categorization, and discrepancies within certain NGQSS and LIDAROC records. 
However, portions of OPC’s analysis rely on comparisons between datasets tracking related but 
different events (for example, odor complaints versus leaks) serving different operational and 
reporting purposes submitted across different time periods, which makes direct comparison 
inappropriate and inaccurate. The difficulty in comparing related but operationally distinct data 
has been discussed in several technical conferences in Formal Case Nos. 977 and 1178. The fact 
that OPC was able to make its observations based on information in these proceedings 
demonstrates that the Commission is taking proactive steps to review and address WGL’s 
continued noncompliance and identify ways to enhance transparency and accountability. 

20. 
A secondary concern for the Commission to address was the cost of the IDM. OPC 
argues that WGL should not be able to recover the cost of the IDM from ratepayers because WGL’s 
alleged reporting infractions caused the need for the IDM.63 WGL argues that the cost of the IDM 
should be recoverable because it would be considered a prudently incurred cost from an activity 
the Commission orders WGL to undertake.64 At this juncture, the question of cost recovery is not 
ripe for our determination. 

21. 
In Formal Case No. 977, the Commission directs Staff to continue to schedule 
technical conferences as necessary. The Commission expects the technical conferences in Formal 
Case No. 977 to result in compliance with 15 DCMR Chapter 37. The Commission reminds the 
parties that, in Order No. 22722, it has elected to lower the penalty assessed to WGL in favor of 
an approach that creates a direct line of communication between WGL, OPC, and Commission 
Staff through technical conferences to address deficiencies found in NGQSS and LIDAROC
